items.title: Max Stack
items.question: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, peekMax and popMax (remove the largest element; if there are several, the one closest to the top).
items.short: Keep the stack as a doubly linked list so any node can be removed in O(1), plus a TreeMap from value to the nodes holding that value (newest last). push/pop/top are O(1) on the list plus O(log n) on the TreeMap. peekMax is lastKey(). popMax takes the newest node of the largest key, unlinks it from the list, and cleans up the map. Everything is O(log n).
followups: Make every op O(1) amortized except popMax? (Two-stack variants; prove it's impossible to get all O(1): you'd sort in O(n).)
Thread-safe version? (One lock around both structures; operations are short.)
MinMaxStack, or popMax on a queue instead of a stack?

items.title: API request blocker (rate limit + block)
items.source: Sep 9 report ("API Blocking"). Exact wording wasn't reported; this is the common form of the question.
items.question: Allow each client at most `limit` requests per `window` seconds. A client that goes over is blocked for `blockFor` seconds. Implement `allow(clientId, timestamp)`.
items.short: Per client, keep a queue of accepted timestamps and a blockedUntil time. On a request: if blocked, reject. Otherwise drop timestamps older than the window from the front; if the queue still has `limit` entries, block the client (blockedUntil = now + blockFor), clear its history and reject; else record the timestamp and accept. Amortized O(1) per call, O(clients × limit) memory.
followups: Switch to a token bucket: what changes? (Refill tokens lazily from elapsed time; no queue.)
Different limits per API key tier? (A config lookup; key = (client, endpoint).)
Out-of-order timestamps? (Insert into the right place, or accept small skew.)

items.title: Job scheduler (one-time and recurring), in-memory
items.source: Sep 9 report ("Job Scheduler"). The same idea underlies the system design round.
items.question: Support schedule(job, time), scheduleRecurring(job, first, interval), cancel(job) and runUntil(now), returning the runs that are due, in order.
items.short: A min-heap of upcoming runs ordered by (time, jobId). runUntil pops everything due; a recurring run pushes its next occurrence back in. cancel is lazy: bump a version number for the job and skip heap entries whose version is stale. A map of live 'pending' runs answers cancel's return value in O(1). Each operation is O(log n).
followups: Implement it with real threads. (DelayQueue / Condition.awaitNanos; handle spurious wakeups.)
Cron expressions instead of intervals? (A function nextRun(after) replaces time + interval.)
Priorities among jobs due at the same time? (Add priority to the comparator.)

items.title: LRU Cache → Progressive LRU (AI coding round)
items.source: Sep 7 report, Round 3 (AI coding: progressive LRU). AI is meant as an assistant, not a replacement.
items.question: Implement an LRU cache, then extend it step by step (typical steps: expiry/TTL, thread safety, size-based capacity, metrics/eviction callbacks).
items.short: Step 1: HashMap<key, Node> + doubly linked list, with the most recently used at the head; get and put are O(1). Step 2 (TTL): store expireAt in each node; get checks it lazily; put on a full cache drops expired entries before evicting the LRU. A min-heap by expireAt avoids the O(n) sweep. Step 3 (threads): one lock (simple, correct), then striped or segmented locks, or ConcurrentHashMap plus approximate LRU for scale. Step 4: weight-based capacity, eviction listener, hit/miss stats. Keep each step's tests green before moving on.
followups: Why not a read-write lock? (get changes recency, so it's a write.)
LRU vs LFU vs W-TinyLFU: when does LRU do badly? (A scan pollutes the cache; frequency-aware policies resist it.)
Distributed cache: consistent hashing, replication, hot keys.

items.title: Find Leaves of Binary Tree (LC 366) → general graph
items.question: Repeatedly remove all leaves of a binary tree and return the values removed in each round. Follow-up: the structure is a general graph. How does the approach change?
items.short: Tree: a node is removed in round = its height (leaf = 0). One post-order DFS computes the height and appends the node to out[height]: O(n). Graph: there's no root, nodes can have several parents, and there may be cycles. Height-by-DFS double-counts shared children (memoize) and loops forever on cycles. Use Kahn's algorithm on reversed edges: start from nodes with no children, remove them, and decrement their parents' child counts level by level. Nodes on (or above) a cycle never become leaves; report them.
followups: Return the remaining cycle nodes too. (Everything with remaining children > 0.)
Edges arrive as a stream (dependency updates)? (Incremental counts; recompute affected layers.)
Where does this show up for real? (Build systems and package managers: which modules can be built or deleted first.)

items.title: Robot in an unexplored grid
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 4: rotate, move forward, detect walls, reposition to explored cells; find a path to the target.
items.question: The grid isn't given. A robot API lets you rotate, move forward (reporting walls), check for the target, and jump back to explored cells. Find the shortest path from the start to the target.
items.short: Build your own map in coordinates relative to the start (the start is (0,0)). Because reposition lets you jump to any explored cell, you can run BFS directly: pop a cell, reposition there, and for each direction not yet known, turn to face it and try moveForward. If it moves, record the neighbour at distance + 1 and reposition back. The first time isTarget() is true, the BFS depth is the shortest path. Without reposition: DFS with backtracking to map the reachable area, then BFS on the map.
followups: What if turning costs time? (State = (cell, facing); Dijkstra or 0-1 BFS.)
What if the grid is huge and the target is close? (BFS stops early; A* once the target is known.)
Make the exploration resumable after a crash? (Persist the map.)

items.title: Supply drop: nearest supply, then a constrained route (AI-assisted graph round)
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 2. Part 1 was reported; part 2 "reasoned about a transformed version of the graph with additional structural constraints" and wasn't remembered exactly. Part II here is the most likely shape; the other likely twists are covered below.
items.question: Locations connected by routes; some have supplies. Part 1: distance from the landing location to the nearest suitable supply location. Part 2: a harder version on a transformed graph with extra constraints.
items.short: Part 1 is single-source shortest path: Dijkstra from the landing site (BFS if routes are unweighted), stopping at the first supply location popped. Part 2's 'transformed graph' is almost certainly a **state graph**: each node becomes (location, extra state). Examples: (location, hasSupplies) for 'must visit a supply first', (location, fuelLeft) for limited fuel, (location, stopsUsed) for a hop limit, or reversed edges for 'distance from every location to the nearest supply'. Run the same Dijkstra or BFS over the states.
followups: Return the actual route. (Keep a parent pointer per state; walk back from the goal state.)
Supplies get used up (each depot serves one team)? (Assignment / min-cost matching, not shortest path.)
Distances change while the team is moving? (Re-run from the current location; incremental algorithms like D* Lite.)

items.title: CI build pipeline: minimum total time (topological sort)
items.source: Aug 11 report ("CI/CD, Job Scheduling"). A natural coding question for a CI/CD team; also the core of the CI scheduler design.
items.question: Jobs with durations and dependencies run in parallel. When does the pipeline finish? Detect cycles.
items.short: Kahn's topological sort. A job's earliest start = max finish time of its dependencies; the answer is the max finish time (the critical path). If fewer than n jobs get processed, there's a cycle → -1. O(V + E).
followups: Detect *which* jobs form the cycle. (DFS with colours; report the back edge.)
Minimum time with k workers. (Heuristic; explain NP-hardness.)
Jobs can be cached; how do you decide a job can be skipped? (Hash of inputs + toolchain.)

items.title: Distributed job scheduler (one-time and recurring jobs): full design
items.source: Sep 9 report, Round 2 (must support one-time and recurring jobs). Also the base for the Aug 11 CI scheduler round.
items.question: Design a job scheduling system that supports one-time jobs and recurring jobs.
items.short: Jobs and runs live in a sharded store; a recurring job only ever has its next occurrence as a run row. Runs are hashed into thousands of partitions; a coordinator leases partitions (with an epoch/fencing token) to scheduler nodes, which load runs due in the next few minutes into an in-memory timer. When a run is due, the node moves it SCHEDULED → QUEUED with a conditional write (and inserts the next occurrence in the same transaction, idempotent via UNIQUE(job_id, scheduled_at)), but only after acquiring QoS capacity for the run's job type (rate token + concurrency slot); without capacity the run is deferred, not failed. then enqueues it. Executors pull, hold a heartbeat lease, call the target with run_id as the idempotency key, and report back; a reaper retries runs whose lease expired, with exponential backoff and jitter, ending in DEAD + alert. Delivery is at-least-once, never lost, and duplicates are prevented by fencing. Then cover misfire/overlap policies, DST, the top-of-the-hour spike (look-ahead, batching, jitter, quotas), scheduling-lag SLOs, multi-region failover and a phased rollout.
items.answer:
### How to run this in 45 minutes
| Minutes | What you do | What to draw |
|---|---|---|
| 0–5 | Requirements and scope; agree on numbers | a short list on the board |
| 5–8 | Estimates (runs/sec, peak, storage) | 3 numbers |
| 8–12 | API + data model | the `jobs` and `job_runs` tables |
| 12–22 | High-level architecture; walk one job end to end | the architecture diagram |
| 22–40 | Deep dives: due-time index, no double-firing, recurring jobs, **retries with exponential backoff**, **QoS and throttling per job type**, the top-of-the-hour spike | state machine + partition ownership + QoS layers |
| 40–45 | Scale, multi-region, operations, what you'd build first | phased plan |
Say the plan out loud at the start. Interviewers at Staff level score how you **drive** the session as much as the boxes.

### 1. Requirements
**Functional**
- Create a **one-time** job: run at a given time (or "now + delay").
- Create a **recurring** job: a cron expression (`0 9 * * MON-FRI`) or a fixed interval, in a **time zone**, with optional start and end dates.
- The job's target: call an HTTP endpoint, publish to a queue, or run a container/function with a payload.
- Update, pause, resume, delete a job; trigger it manually.
- Every job has a **job type** (e.g. `email-send`, `report-generation`, `billing-charge`). Each type carries a **QoS profile**: a class (critical / standard / best-effort), a rate limit, max concurrency (overall and per tenant) and a start deadline, so the platform can **throttle** each kind of work and protect the systems it calls.
- Failed runs are **retried with exponential backoff and jitter**, only for retryable errors, up to a max attempts / max duration, then dead-lettered with an alert.
- Per-job policies: timeout, what to do with missed runs (misfire), whether runs may overlap.
- Run history: every execution with status, attempts, timings, error, and a link to logs.

**Non-functional**
- **Reliability:** an accepted job never silently fails to run. No lost runs.
- **No duplicate runs** in normal operation; delivery to the target is at-least-once under failures, so a run carries an idempotency key.
- **Timeliness, per QoS class:** critical runs start within ~1–2 s of their scheduled time at p99, standard within ~30 s, best-effort whenever capacity allows (agree on these; they drive the design).
- **Isolation:** one team's or one job type's surge must not delay critical work or overload a downstream service.
- **Scale:** horizontally scalable, multi-tenant, highly available (no single scheduler box).
- **Observability** for job owners and for operators.

**Out of scope (say it):** workflow DAGs with data passing (Airflow/Temporal territory, mention as an extension), sub-second precision, running arbitrary user code securely (we call targets; container execution is a pluggable executor).

### 2. Estimates
Assume a company-wide platform:
- **50M active job definitions** (most are recurring).
- **~500M runs/day** → ~**6k runs/s on average**.
- **Peak is the problem:** cron times cluster at :00 and :30 and at midnight. Assume **10× average at the top of the hour: ~60k runs/s** for a few seconds.
- Job definition ~2 KB → **~100 GB**: fits on a modest sharded database.
- Run record ~0.5 KB × 500M/day → **~250 GB/day**. Keep 30 days hot (~7.5 TB, sharded), archive older history to object storage.
- Each run causes ~4–5 state writes (scheduled → queued → running → done) → **~30k writes/s average, 300k/s peak**. This is why the run store must be partitioned and the hot path batched.

Executors use an internal API: `claim`, `heartbeat(runId, leaseToken)`, `complete(runId, leaseToken, result)`.

### 4. Data model
**jobs**: one row per definition (source of truth), sharded by `job_id`
| column | notes |
|---|---|
| job_id (PK), tenant_id, owner | |
| schedule_type, cron / interval / run_at, timezone, start_at, end_at | |
| **job_type**, qos_override | QoS profile comes from job_types; override may only *lower* the class |
| target (JSON), retry (JSON), policy (JSON) | backoff parameters, timeout, misfire, overlap |
| status | ACTIVE / PAUSED / DELETED |
| version | bumped on every update; a run remembers the version it was created from |
| next_run_at | denormalized for display |

**job_runs**: one row per scheduled execution, sharded by `job_id`, so a job's runs sit together
| column | notes |
|---|---|
| run_id (PK) | |
| job_id, **scheduled_at** | **UNIQUE(job_id, scheduled_at)**: the key that prevents duplicate runs |
| partition | hash(job_id) mod P, used by the due index |
| state | see the state machine below |
| **qos_class**, job_type | denormalized so the dispatcher can throttle without a lookup |
| attempt, next_attempt_at, last_error_class | retries and backoff |
| throttle_count, deferred_until | how often QoS deferred it (doesn't use up attempts) |
| lease_owner, lease_token, lease_expires_at | which executor holds it |
| started_at, ended_at, error, result_ref | |

**job_types**: the QoS registry (small, cached in every scheduler and executor node)
| column | notes |
|---|---|
| job_type (PK), owner_team | |
| qos_class | CRITICAL / STANDARD / BEST_EFFORT, each with a start-lag SLO and a guaranteed capacity share |
| rate_limit_per_sec, burst | token bucket for the whole type |
| max_concurrency, max_concurrency_per_tenant | in-flight runs |
| target_key | shared downstream limits (several types → one service) |
| start_deadline_sec, preemptible, executor_pool | |
| retry_defaults | initialDelay, multiplier, maxDelay, maxAttempts, retryOn |

**Due index**: the structure the scheduler reads. Logically it maps `(partition, due_time) → run_id` for runs in state SCHEDULED. Physically it's a secondary index `(partition, state, due_at)` on job_runs, or its own table bucketed by minute (`partition, minute_bucket → run_ids`) in Cassandra/DynamoDB.

**Key idea for recurring jobs:** only the **next** occurrence of a recurring job exists as a row. When it's dispatched, the scheduler inserts the following occurrence. There is never an infinite or pre-expanded series.

**One job end to end** (the numbers match the diagram):
1. The client creates a job. The API validates the cron expression, checks quotas, and in one transaction writes the `jobs` row and the **first `job_runs` row** (state SCHEDULED, `scheduled_at` = first occurrence).
2. The scheduler node that owns that run's partition **loads** runs due in the next few minutes into an in-memory timer.
3. When the timer fires, the dispatcher first **acquires QoS capacity** for the run's job type (a rate token and a concurrency slot). If there's none, the run is **deferred**: it stays SCHEDULED with a short delay, not failed. Otherwise it moves the run SCHEDULED → QUEUED with a **conditional update** (only if still SCHEDULED, with its partition epoch), and for a recurring job **inserts the next occurrence** in the same transaction.
4. It publishes the run to the queue for its **QoS class**.
5. An executor pulls it, takes a **lease** (RUNNING, lease_expires_at = now + 30 s), and calls the target with `Idempotency-Key: run_id`.
6. The executor heartbeats while working and reports the result.
7. The status service records SUCCEEDED / FAILED, releases the concurrency slot, schedules a retry with **exponential backoff** if the error is retryable, and the **lease reaper** recovers runs whose executor died.
8. Metrics and events feed dashboards, the run-history UI, and alerts to job owners.

Every transition is a **conditional write** ("UPDATE … WHERE state = <expected> AND lease_token = <mine>"). Two actors racing on the same run can't both win.

### 7. Deep dive: finding due runs fast (the core)
Options, simplest first:
| Approach | How | Good for | Limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DB polling** | `SELECT … WHERE state='SCHEDULED' AND due_at <= now() ORDER BY due_at LIMIT 500 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` | v1, up to a few thousand runs/s; very simple | index hot spot, polling load, lag = poll interval |
| **Time-bucketed table** | key `(partition, minute_bucket)` → run_ids in Cassandra/DynamoDB; read the current and next bucket | very high write rates, cheap | only minute granularity without the next layer |
| **Redis sorted set per partition** | `ZADD due:{p} <ts> run_id`; `ZRANGEBYSCORE … 0 now` | low latency | needs durability story (AOF, rebuild from DB) |
| **In-memory timer per partition owner** | the owner loads "due within 5 min" from the store into a min-heap or **hierarchical timing wheel** | sub-second precision, no polling per run | must reload on ownership change |

**Recommendation:** the durable store is the source of truth (row + due index, bucketed by partition and minute), and each partition owner keeps an **in-memory timer for the next ~5 minutes**, refilled by a loader every ~30 s. Runs created for "now" are pushed straight to the owner's timer (or picked up by the next load). This gives timeliness without polling the database per run, and a node restart only needs to reload one window.

A **timing wheel** (Kafka and Netty use them) is an array of slots, one per second, each holding a list of runs. Insert and expiry are O(1); a min-heap is O(log n) and is fine too. Name both.

### 8. Deep dive: partitioning and never firing twice
- Hash each run's `job_id` into **P virtual partitions** (e.g. 4096). Many more partitions than nodes makes rebalancing smooth.
- A **coordinator** (etcd / ZooKeeper, or a lease table) assigns partitions to scheduler nodes. Each assignment is a **lease with an epoch** (a fencing token) that increases every time ownership changes.
- The dispatcher's write includes the epoch: `UPDATE job_runs SET state='QUEUED' WHERE run_id=? AND state='SCHEDULED'` plus a check that the partition's current epoch equals mine. A paused or partitioned "zombie" node that still thinks it owns the partition fails this write. That's **fencing**, and it's the answer to "what if two schedulers think they own the same partition?".
- The `UNIQUE(job_id, scheduled_at)` constraint makes inserting the next occurrence **idempotent**: if two nodes try, one insert fails harmlessly.
- **Exactly-once execution isn't achievable end to end** without the target's cooperation. A worker can finish the work and die before reporting. So the contract is: the scheduler creates each run exactly once, delivers it **at least once**, and sends `run_id` as an idempotency key so targets can dedupe. Say this clearly; it's what interviewers want to hear.

### 9. Deep dive: recurring jobs done right
- **Next occurrence only.** On dispatch of run N, compute `next = cron.nextAfter(scheduled_at_N)` in the job's time zone and insert run N+1 **in the same transaction**. Compute from the *scheduled* time, not from "now", so delays don't make the schedule drift.
- **Time zones and DST:** store the cron expression plus an IANA zone. On the spring-forward day 02:30 doesn't exist (run at 03:00, or skip). On the fall-back day 01:30 happens twice (run once). Pick and document the rule.
- **Misfire policy** after an outage (the scheduler was down from 1:00 to 4:00 for an hourly job): `run_once` (one catch-up run now, default), `run_all` (backfill each missed run, capped), or `skip` (jump to the next future time).
- **Overlap policy** when the previous run is still RUNNING: `allow`, `skip` (record SKIPPED), or `queue` (start after it finishes). Needs a quick lookup of the job's active run.
- **Updates and pauses:** updating the schedule bumps `jobs.version`; the dispatcher compares the run's version to the job's and replaces stale future runs. Pause = mark the job PAUSED, and the dispatcher skips its runs (or deletes the future one; on resume, apply the misfire policy).
- **Fixed rate vs fixed delay** for interval jobs: next = scheduled + interval vs finish + interval. Offer both.

### 10. Deep dive: execution, failures and retries
- **Pull model:** executors pull from queues. That gives back-pressure, per-pool autoscaling on queue depth, and pools per target type (HTTP callers, container runners, GPU). Push (the dispatcher calls the target directly) is simpler for HTTP-only systems but you lose buffering.
- **Leases:** claiming sets `lease_expires_at = now + 30 s` and a random `lease_token`. Heartbeats every 10 s extend it. A **reaper** scans for expired leases and moves those runs to FAILED attempt → retry. A worker reporting with an old token is ignored (fencing again).
- **Timeouts:** the executor enforces `timeoutSec` (kills the container or aborts the HTTP call) and reports TIMED_OUT.
- **Retries:** see the next section.
- **Poison jobs:** a job that fails every time gets auto-paused after N consecutive dead runs, and the owner is notified.
- **Cancelling a running run:** a control message to the executor holding the lease (a cancel flag checked with each heartbeat response).

### 11. Deep dive: retries with exponential backoff
**Why exponential, and why jitter.** Most failures are transient (a deploy, a blip, an overloaded dependency). Retrying immediately turns one failure into a storm. Waiting longer after each failure gives the dependency time to recover. **Jitter** spreads the retries out: when a downstream outage fails 50,000 runs at the same second, retries without jitter would all come back at the same second again (a thundering herd).

**The formula** (per job type defaults, overridable per job):
```
delay(attempt) = min(maxDelay, initialDelay × multiplier^(attempt - 1))
full jitter:   wait = random(0, delay)                 // spreads best; AWS's recommendation
equal jitter:  wait = delay/2 + random(0, delay/2)     // keeps a minimum wait
next_attempt_at = now + wait   (or the server's Retry-After, if larger)
```
Example: initialDelay 30 s, multiplier 2, maxDelay 1 h, maxAttempts 6:
| failed attempt | base delay | with full jitter |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 30 s | 0–30 s |
| 2 | 1 min | 0–1 min |
| 3 | 2 min | 0–2 min |
| 4 | 4 min | 0–4 min |
| 5 | 8 min | 0–8 min |
| 6 | | → **DEAD**, alert owner |
Also cap the **total** retry time (`maxRetryDurationSec`), so a job doesn't keep retrying long after its result is useful.

**Which failures to retry** (classify the error, don't retry blindly):
| Error | Retry? |
|---|---|
| 5xx, connection refused/reset, timeout | yes, with backoff |
| 429 Too Many Requests / 503 with `Retry-After` | yes; wait at least `Retry-After`, and tell the QoS limiter the target is saturated |
| executor lost (lease expired) | yes (counts as an attempt; target dedupes on run_id) |
| 400 / 401 / 403 / 404, validation error | **no**: fail fast to DEAD; retrying can't fix it |
| job's own "permanent failure" signal | no |

**How it's implemented** (durable, no sleeping threads):
1. The executor reports FAILED with an **error class**.
2. The status service computes `next_attempt_at`, and with one conditional write sets `state = SCHEDULED, attempt = attempt + 1, due_at = next_attempt_at` (only if the lease token matches).
3. The retry goes back through the **same due index and timers** as any scheduled run. It survives restarts, and it's subject to QoS throttling like everything else.
4. The idempotency key stays `run_id` for every attempt, so the target can dedupe a retry of work that actually succeeded.

```
static long backoffMillis(int attempt, long initialMs, double multiplier, long maxMs, Random rnd) {
    double base = initialMs * Math.pow(multiplier, attempt - 1);
    long capped = (long) Math.min((double) maxMs, base);
    return (long) (rnd.nextDouble() * capped);          // full jitter
}
```

**Interactions to mention**
- **Recurring jobs:** if the next occurrence comes due while run N is still retrying, the overlap policy decides: usually the new occurrence **supersedes** the old retries (a stale hourly report isn't worth retrying). Keep maxRetryDuration below the interval.
- **Retry budget:** retries may use at most ~10–20% of a job type's capacity. When a downstream is down, retries shouldn't crowd out fresh work.
- **Circuit breaker per target_key:** after many failures in a row, open the circuit and **defer** that type's runs (QoS deferral, no attempts used) for a cool-down period instead of burning every run's attempts against a dead service. Half-open: let a few runs through to probe.
- **Poison jobs:** N consecutive DEAD runs → auto-pause the job and notify the owner.
- **DLQ and replay:** DEAD runs are kept with their last error; owners can replay one or many after fixing the cause.

### 12. Deep dive: QoS per job type and throttling
**Why per job type.** Throttling individual jobs doesn't work: limits are really about the **kind of work** and **the downstream it hits**. 10,000 different jobs of type `email-send` together must not exceed the email provider's limit, and `billing-charge` must start on time even while a best-effort backfill floods the system.

**QoS classes**
| Class | Start-lag SLO (p99) | Guaranteed share | Under overload | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CRITICAL | ~2 s | reserved capacity (e.g. 30%) | never shed; may preempt best-effort | billing charge, security key rotation |
| STANDARD | ~30 s | weighted share | deferred if over its type's limit | reports, notifications |
| BEST_EFFORT | hours OK | leftovers only | shed first, preemptible | backfills, cleanups, ML batch scoring |
Teams can't mark their own jobs CRITICAL: the class comes from the job type, which the platform approves. A job may only lower its class.

**Where throttling happens** (defence in depth):
1. **Admission (API):** quotas per tenant on how many jobs and how many runs/day they can create. Reject at create time with a clear error.
2. **Dispatch (main control point):** before SCHEDULED → QUEUED the dispatcher must acquire:
   a **rate token** from the job type's token bucket (and the tenant × type bucket), and a **concurrency slot** for the type (and the target_key).
   If either is missing, the run is **deferred**: it stays SCHEDULED in the in-memory timer with a short delay (e.g. 1–5 s with jitter), `throttle_count + 1`, **no attempt used**. If it can't start before `startDeadlineSec`, it becomes EXPIRED (skipped and reported) rather than building an endless backlog.
3. **Queues per class:** executors pull with **weighted priority** (e.g. 70 / 25 / 5) plus aging, so best-effort never starves completely but can't delay critical work.
4. **Execution:** separate executor pools per class (or per type for heavy work); concurrency slots are released when the run finishes or its lease expires (the reaper frees leaked slots).

**Distributed token buckets** (many scheduler nodes share one limit per type):
- **Central limiter:** a Redis token bucket per type with an atomic Lua script (refill by elapsed time, take N tokens). Dispatchers ask for tokens **in batches** (e.g. 50 at a time) to keep Redis calls low.
- **Or leased budgets:** the coordinator splits each type's rate among scheduler nodes in proportion to the partitions they own and re-balances every few seconds. Purely local checks, a little less exact.
- **Concurrency slots:** a counter per type/target with lease-tied entries (slot = run_id with expiry), so a crashed executor's slot comes back automatically.

**Adaptive throttling for downstream health:** static limits are a ceiling; the **effective** limit adapts. Per target_key, use AIMD on concurrency: on 429/5xx/high latency, cut the limit by half; on success, add +1 per interval. Combined with the circuit breaker from the retry section, this protects a struggling service automatically.

**Overload and load shedding order:** (1) defer BEST_EFFORT, preempting preemptible runs if needed, (2) defer STANDARD over-limit types, (3) never shed CRITICAL; page if CRITICAL lag breaks its SLO. Make the order explicit; interviewers ask.

**Observability for QoS:** per type: throttled runs/s, deferral time, in-flight vs limit, start lag vs class SLO, expired runs. Alert the type owner when they're **consistently** throttled (they need a higher limit or fewer jobs), and the platform when a class misses its SLO.

### 13. Deep dive: the top-of-the-hour spike and multi-tenancy
- 60k runs/s for a few seconds at :00. The **look-ahead** means the owners already hold these runs in memory before :00, so there's no database scan at the critical moment, only the conditional writes and enqueues, batched (one write per 100 runs).
- **Pre-dispatch:** runs can be enqueued a few seconds early into a delay-capable queue (SQS delay of up to 15 minutes, Kafka delay topics) so executors start exactly on time.
- **Jitter option:** let owners opt in to "any time within this 5-minute window". It flattens the spike dramatically; offer it as the default for new jobs.
- **Fairness:** the QoS layer above does the heavy lifting: per-type and per-tenant token buckets, class queues with weighted priority, so one team's 1M-run backfill (BEST_EFFORT) doesn't delay another team's critical job.
- **Capacity:** 60k/s across 4096 partitions on ~40 scheduler nodes ≈ 1.5k dispatches/s per node, well within one node's reach. The run store's write throughput is the real limit, which is why runs are sharded and writes batched.

### 14. Reliability, multi-region, operations
- **Store:** a sharded SQL database (Vitess/Aurora) or a wide-column store (Cassandra/DynamoDB) with replication across availability zones. SQL gives you transactions for "mark dispatched + insert next run"; with a NoSQL store you use conditional writes and make the next-run insert idempotent.
- **Scheduler node failure:** its partition leases expire (~10 s), the coordinator reassigns them, and new owners load the window **including a look-back** (runs that are due but still SCHEDULED). Worst case: a run starts ~10–15 s late, never lost.
- **Multi-region:** usually **active-passive per job**: each job has a home region, with the store replicated asynchronously. On failover the other region takes over partitions and applies the misfire policy to the gap. Active-active needs globally consistent run creation (Spanner, or a per-job home region), which is usually not worth it.
- **Clock skew:** compare due times against the scheduler's clock (NTP-synced). Small skew only shifts a run by milliseconds; fencing protects correctness, not clocks.
- **Observability (Staff signal):** **scheduling lag** (actual start − scheduled time) at p50/p99 per partition, success and failure rates per tenant, queue depth and wait, lease expiries, dead runs. A run-history UI for owners, alerts routed to the owning team, and an audit log of job changes.
- **Operational controls:** pause-all switch (per tenant or global), drain a partition, replay or backfill a time range, rate limits.
- **Security:** authN/Z on the API per tenant; secrets referenced by ID (not stored in payloads); executors call targets with scoped credentials; container jobs run sandboxed.

### 15. Trade-offs to say out loud
- **Polling a database vs in-memory timers:** simplicity vs timeliness and database load. Start with polling; move to partitioned timers when you outgrow it.
- **SQL vs NoSQL for runs:** transactions vs write scale.
- **At-least-once + idempotency vs exactly-once:** exactly-once needs the target in the same transaction, so it's rarely possible.
- **Pull vs push execution.**
- **Central vs leased token buckets:** exact limits with an extra network hop vs local decisions with slight overshoot.
- **Defer vs reject when throttled:** deferring keeps work safe but can build a backlog, so pair it with start deadlines (EXPIRED) and per-type alerts.
- **Pre-materializing runs** (e.g. 24 h ahead: easy queries and visibility) vs **next-occurrence only** (less storage; updates are trivial). I chose next-only, with a window preview computed on read for the UI.
- **Build vs buy:** Quartz (DB locks; fine for one service), Kubernetes CronJob (cluster-scoped), AWS EventBridge Scheduler, Temporal timers (durable workflows), Airflow (data DAGs). Building makes sense for a company-wide multi-tenant platform with custom executors and SLOs.

### 16. How I'd roll it out (phased plan)
1. **v1 (weeks):** one sharded SQL database, DB polling with `SKIP LOCKED`, an HTTP executor, retries with exponential backoff, run history, job types with static rate and concurrency limits. Handles thousands of runs/s.
2. **v2:** partitions + coordinator + in-memory timers, Kafka queues per QoS class, executor pools, distributed token buckets, retry budgets and circuit breakers, scheduling-lag SLOs per class.
3. **v3:** adaptive (AIMD) throttling per downstream, preemption of best-effort work, multi-region failover, workflow dependencies (job B after A), self-serve UI, cost attribution per team.

### 17. Extensions they may ask about
- **Dependencies / DAGs:** a run becomes SCHEDULED only when its upstream runs succeed (counters per downstream run, like topological sort); see the CI scheduler design.
- **Delayed messages at huge scale (hundreds of thousands/s, short delays):** a dedicated timing-wheel delay service in front of Kafka instead of a database row per message.
- **Exactly-once to Kafka targets:** transactional producer + idempotent consumers.
followups: Two scheduler nodes both think they own partition 17. What happens? (Epoch fencing on every write; the stale node's CAS fails.)
A worker finished the job but died before reporting. (Lease expires → retry → the target dedupes on run_id. At-least-once.)
How do you show the next 10 runs of a cron job in the UI if only one is stored? (Compute them from the cron expression on read.)
The run store is the bottleneck at :00. (Batch conditional writes, pre-load, jitter opt-in, separate hot run state from cold history.)
How would you add 'job B runs after job A succeeds'? (Dependency counters on downstream runs; DAG engine.)
One job type gets throttled all day. What do you do? (It's a capacity signal: alert the owner, raise its limit if the downstream can take it, or add a start deadline so stale runs expire.)
Why jitter on backoff? (A downstream outage fails thousands of runs at once; without jitter their retries arrive together again.)
Do throttled runs use up retry attempts? (No: deferral isn't failure. Only executed attempts count.)
Why not Kubernetes CronJob / Quartz? (Cluster- or app-scoped, DB lock contention, no multi-tenant quotas or SLOs.)

items.title: CI job scheduler (build system): triggers, scheduling, live logs
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 3. The CI-specific follow-ups were the hard part: (1) how live stdout from running jobs reaches the UI; (2) how repository changes trigger CI: push-based webhooks vs CI-side polling.
items.question: Design a job scheduler for a continuous-integration system. Follow-ups: surfacing live build output in the UI; integrating with the Git host (webhooks vs polling).
items.short: Pipeline: Git host event → trigger service (dedupe, find the pipeline config in the repo) → pipeline DAG of jobs → scheduler matches ready jobs to runner pools by labels (OS, GPU, size) with per-org fairness → runners pull work, run in fresh containers or VMs, stream logs and heartbeats → results posted back to the PR as commit statuses. Live logs: runners send log chunks to a log service that appends to a per-job stream (in memory or Redis, then object storage) and fans out to browsers over WebSocket/SSE, with offset-based resume. Triggers: webhooks for latency (verify signatures, handle retries, dedupe by delivery id) plus periodic polling or reconciliation as a safety net for missed events.
items.answer:
### 1. Requirements
- Triggers: push, pull request (opened or updated), tag, manual run, schedule (nightly).
- Pipeline defined **in the repo** (`.ci.yml`): stages and jobs, dependencies, runner labels, caches, artifacts, secrets.
- Jobs run in **isolated** environments (containers or VMs) on runner pools (linux-x64, mac, gpu …).
- Live logs in the UI, final status on the PR, artifacts and test reports, cancel and re-run.
- Scale assumption: 50k engineers, 200k pipelines/day, 2M jobs/day, peak ~100 jobs/sec started; median job 5 min.

### 2. Architecture
```
Git host ──webhook──► Trigger service ──► Pipeline service ──► Scheduler ──► Runner pools (pull)
   ▲   (or poller)        dedupe, read          build DAG,        ready queue     ephemeral containers / VMs
   │                      .ci.yml at SHA        persist runs      per pool, fair      │ heartbeats, status
   │                                                              share per org       │ log chunks
   └──── commit status / checks API ◄─── Results service ◄────────────────────────────┤
                                                                                       ▼
                                     Browser ◄──WebSocket/SSE── Log service ──► object storage (archive)
```

### 3. Scheduling (the core)
- **Pipeline = DAG** of jobs (topological order; see the "CI build pipeline" coding problem). When a job succeeds, decrement its dependents' counts; jobs at 0 become **READY**.
- **Matching:** READY jobs go into a queue per runner label set. Runners **pull** (long-poll `/jobs/next?labels=…`), which gives natural back-pressure and works through firewalls (self-hosted runners only need outbound access).
- **Fairness:** one org or monorepo mustn't starve the others. Use weighted fair queuing per org/repo, concurrency limits per project, and higher priority for PR checks than for nightly runs.
- **Leases and heartbeats:** a claimed job has a lease; a missed heartbeat marks the runner dead and the job is **retried** (or marked failed for non-idempotent deploy jobs).
- **Cancellation and superseding:** a new push to the same PR cancels in-flight runs for the old SHA (saves a lot of compute).
- **Autoscaling** runner pools on queue depth and wait time; warm pools for fast start.
- **Caching:** dependency caches and remote build caches keyed by lockfile hash; artifact passing between jobs through object storage.

### 4. Follow-up: surfacing live build output
Requirements: a few seconds of latency, survives page reloads, many viewers per job, very long logs (100 MB+), and the log is kept after the job ends.
1. **Runner side:** an agent wraps the process and captures stdout and stderr. It batches lines into **chunks** (every ~1 s or 64 KB), each with a sequence number, and sends them to the log service over HTTP/2 or gRPC streaming. It buffers locally and retries if the network blips (at-least-once; the sequence number dedupes).
2. **Log service:** appends chunks to a per-job stream: the **hot tier** is Redis Streams, Kafka, or an in-memory ring buffer on the owning node (shard by job_id). When the job finishes, the whole log is written to **object storage** (S3), compressed, as the cold tier.
3. **Browser:** opens a **WebSocket or Server-Sent Events** connection with `fromOffset`. It gets the backlog first, then live chunks. On reconnect it resumes from the last offset. Viewers of finished jobs read directly from object storage (CDN, range requests for huge logs).
4. **Fan-out:** a pub/sub channel per job_id, so many viewers don't each hit the runner.
5. **Extras:** secret masking in the agent **before** upload, ANSI colour handling, collapsible log sections, size limits and truncation, search.
Why not let the UI poll the runner directly? Runners are ephemeral and often behind NAT; you'd lose logs on crash and couldn't scale viewers.

### 5. Follow-up: repository integration, push vs pull
| | **Push: webhooks** | **Pull: CI polls the Git host** |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | seconds | poll interval (30 s – 5 min) |
| Load | event-driven, cheap | API calls even when nothing changed; rate limits with many repos |
| Reliability | events can be lost (endpoint down; delivery retries are limited) | self-healing: it eventually sees the new ref state |
| Network | the Git host must reach the CI (public endpoint or relay) | only outbound from the CI (good for on-prem CI with SaaS Git) |
| Setup | register a webhook or app per repo/org, manage secrets | credentials to read the repos |
**Good answer: both.** Webhooks for latency, plus a **periodic reconciliation poll** (`ls-remote` or refs API, compare the head SHA with the last built SHA) to catch missed events.

Webhook handling details:
- Verify the **HMAC signature**; respond 2xx **fast** and process asynchronously (put the event on a queue).
- **Idempotency:** dedupe on the delivery id and on (repo, ref, SHA). Webhooks are at-least-once and can arrive out of order, so compare SHAs, don't trust arrival order.
- Read `.ci.yml` **at that commit SHA**, not at the branch head.
- Report back through the commit-status / checks API (pending → success/failure) with a link to the run. Required checks gate merges; a **merge queue** builds the PR rebased on the latest main.
- Integration models: a repo-level webhook; an **app installation** (org-wide, fine-grained permissions, short-lived tokens; preferred); or the Git host's own runner protocol (agents pull from the host).

### 6. Security and isolation (CI is a big attack surface)
Untrusted PR code from forks: no secrets, isolated runners, separate pools. Ephemeral runners (fresh VM or container per job). Scoped short-lived credentials (OIDC tokens to cloud). Signed artifacts and provenance (SLSA).

### 7. Metrics
Queue wait time p95 per pool (the main developer-experience metric), job duration, flake rate, cache hit rate, cost per pipeline, webhook-to-start latency.
followups: A monorepo with 10k targets: how do you avoid running everything on each commit? (Affected-target analysis from the build graph; remote cache.)
How do you handle flaky tests? (Auto-retry once, flake tracking, quarantine with an owner.)
How do deployments (CD) differ from CI jobs? (Not idempotent, serialized per environment, approvals, rollback; see the CI/CD domain notes.)

items.title: User activity collection platform (queries over last 1 min / 1 hour / 1 day)
items.source: Sep 7 report, Round 1: end-to-end flow from API through middleware and storage to the query path; focus on storing and retrieving activity efficiently.
items.question: Design a system that collects user activity events and answers queries over recent windows: last 1 minute, last 1 hour, last 1 day.
items.short: Ingest through a thin API into Kafka (partitioned by user_id). Stream processors pre-aggregate into time buckets at several granularities, e.g. per-second or per-10-s buckets for the last minute, per-minute buckets for the last hour, per-hour (or 5-minute) buckets for the last day. They're stored in a fast KV/time-series store keyed by (entity, metric, bucket). A window query sums at most ~60 buckets; the edge of the window is handled with finer buckets. Raw events go to a data lake for ad-hoc and longer queries. Discuss exact vs approximate (HyperLogLog for distinct users), late events, hot keys, retention, and the read path's latency.
items.answer:
### 1. Clarify (this round is about the query shape)
- What's an "activity"? Page views, clicks, likes, logins. Event = {user_id, type, object_id, ts, attributes}.
- What queries? Per user ("how many profile views did I get in the last hour"), per object, global ("logins in the last minute"), counts vs **distinct** users vs top-K.
- Freshness: seconds. Latency: p99 < 100 ms for windowed reads.
- Scale assumption: 500M DAU, ~50 events/user/day → 25B events/day ≈ **300k events/s average, ~1M/s peak**; ~200 bytes each → 5 TB/day raw.

### 2. API
```
POST /v1/events           batch of events (client SDK batches every few seconds)
GET  /v1/activity/count?entity=user:42&metric=profile_view&window=1h
GET  /v1/activity/top?metric=post_like&window=1d&k=100
```

### 3. Write path
```
clients/services ─► Ingest API (stateless, validates, auth, adds server ts)
                       │  async, ack after Kafka write
                       ▼
                 Kafka topic "activity" (partition by entity id, 3× replication, 7-day retention)
                   ├──► Stream aggregator (Flink / Kafka Streams) ──► Aggregate store (time buckets)
                   └──► Sink to data lake (Parquet on S3, partitioned by date/hour) ──► offline / ad-hoc
```
- The API layer is thin: validate, enrich (server timestamp, geo), batch, write to Kafka. Back-pressure via 429 + client retry.
- **Middleware** = Kafka: decouples spiky writes from storage, allows replay to rebuild aggregates.

### 4. Storage: the key design decision
Don't scan raw events per query. **Pre-aggregate into time buckets** at several resolutions:

| Window | Bucket size | Buckets summed per query | Retention of that resolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| last 1 minute | 1 s (or 5 s) | 60 (or 12) | ~2 minutes |
| last 1 hour | 1 minute | 60 | ~2 hours |
| last 1 day | 1 hour (+ minutes for the edge) | 24 (+ up to 60) | ~2 days |
| longer | 1 day | | months, then the data lake |

- Key: `(entity, metric, resolution, bucket_start) → count` in a store with fast writes and range reads: **Cassandra / ScyllaDB** (partition = entity+metric+resolution+day, clustering = bucket_start), or **Redis** for the hottest short windows, or a time-series DB (Druid / Pinot) when queries need slicing by attributes.
- The window edge: "last hour" at 10:37:20 = minute buckets 09:38…10:36 plus second buckets for 10:37:00–10:37:20 (or accept ±1 bucket of error; ask which).
- **Alternative for small cardinality:** ring buffers in memory (60 slots per resolution per key, like a hit counter: LeetCode 362) sharded by key. Very fast, but you need replication and replay from Kafka for durability.
- **Distinct users:** store a **HyperLogLog** sketch per bucket (≈12 KB, ~1% error) and merge sketches over the window. **Top-K:** Count-Min Sketch + heap per bucket, or the stream processor maintains top-K per window.

### 5. Read path
Query service → computes the bucket list → multi-get from the aggregate store (one partition read) → sums or merges sketches → caches popular results for a second or two. For "last day" with hourly buckets that's ~24–84 values: fast.

### 6. Correctness and edge cases
- **Late or out-of-order events:** use event time with a watermark (e.g. accept up to 2 minutes late); late events update their old bucket.
- **Duplicates:** event_id + idempotent aggregation (exactly-once in Flink with checkpoints + transactional sinks), or accept small over-counts.
- **Hot keys** (a celebrity profile): pre-split counters (key#0..key#N), sum on read; or local pre-aggregation before writing.
- **Retention:** TTL per resolution, so fine buckets expire quickly; that's what keeps storage bounded.
- **Privacy:** user deletion requests (GDPR) need a delete path in raw storage; aggregates are usually non-personal.

### 7. Trade-offs to discuss
Pre-aggregation (fast, fixed queries) vs an OLAP store (flexible slicing, more cost) vs raw scans (cheap to write, slow to read). Exact vs approximate. Freshness vs cost (stream vs micro-batch).
followups: How would you support arbitrary windows (last 17 minutes)? (Combine the coarsest buckets that fit plus finer edges.)
Count distinct users in the last hour? (HyperLogLog per minute bucket, merge 60.)
Rebuild aggregates after a bug? (Replay from Kafka or recompute from the data lake.)

items.title: API blocking / rate limiting at scale
items.source: Sep 9 report ("API Blocking"): the distributed version of the coding problem.
items.question: Design an API-blocking (rate-limiting / abuse-blocking) service in front of many API servers.
items.short: Enforce at the gateway. Keys = (client/API key/IP, endpoint). Counters live in a shared store (Redis cluster sharded by key) and are updated with an atomic Lua script implementing a sliding-window counter or token bucket; blocks are a key with a TTL. For lower latency, give each gateway a local token bucket that syncs periodically, accepting small overshoot. Rules come from a config service. Fail open or closed by endpoint. Return 429 with Retry-After. Abuse blocking adds signals beyond rates (IP reputation, behaviour) and a manual block list.
items.answer:
### Where it runs
API gateway / sidecar on every request → must add < 1–2 ms.

### Design
- **Rules:** `{match: apiKey|ip|user + endpoint, limit, window, blockFor}` from a config service; cached locally, pushed on change.
- **Counter store:** Redis cluster (sharded by key). One **Lua script** per request does: check `block:{key}` → evaluate the sliding-window counter or token bucket → set `block:{key}` with TTL = blockFor when exceeded. Atomic, so there are no races between gateways.
- **Response:** 429 + `Retry-After` + `X-RateLimit-Remaining` headers.

### Latency / availability trade-offs
- **Local + global:** each gateway keeps a local token bucket with a share of the global limit and syncs counts every ~100 ms. Much faster, slight overshoot.
- **Redis down?** Fail **open** for most APIs (availability), fail **closed** for sensitive ones (login, payments).
- Hot keys: a local cache of "blocked" decisions until the TTL expires.

### Abuse blocking (beyond rates)
IP reputation lists, device fingerprints, anomaly detection on behaviour, CAPTCHA challenges instead of hard blocks, a manual block/allow list with audit logging, and a block reason for support.

### Metrics
Rejections per rule, false-positive reports, gateway latency added, Redis latency.
followups: Why a sliding-window counter rather than a log at scale? (2 counters vs O(limit) timestamps per key.)
Multi-region limits? (Per-region budgets, or async cross-region sync with overshoot.)

items.title: CI/CD and developer experience: domain questions
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 1: questions on continuous integration, continuous delivery, package management and developer-infrastructure concepts. Senior Staff needed stronger domain depth here.
items.question: Be ready for rapid-fire domain questions on CI, CD, package management and developer infrastructure.
items.short: Know the vocabulary and the trade-offs, and anchor answers in your own systems. CI: trunk-based development, fast feedback, merge queues, hermetic and cached builds, flaky-test management. CD: artifact promotion, progressive delivery (canary, blue/green, feature flags), automated rollback, DORA metrics. Packages: semantic versioning, lockfiles, dependency resolution (diamond conflicts), private registries, monorepo vs polyrepo. Supply-chain security: SBOM, signing, provenance (SLSA). DevEx: build/test latency and queue time as the north-star metrics.
items.answer:
### Continuous integration
- **CI** = every change is merged to the main line frequently and verified automatically (build + tests). Goal: catch integration problems in minutes, not at release time.
- **Trunk-based development** vs long-lived branches: short-lived branches + feature flags keep merges small.
- **Merge queue:** PRs are tested on top of the latest main (and of each other) before merging, so main stays green with many concurrent merges. Batch and bisect on failure.
- **Fast feedback:** test sharding, running only **affected targets** (build-graph analysis), **remote build caching** (Bazel/Gradle: cache key = hash of inputs + toolchain), **hermetic builds** (no network, pinned toolchains → reproducible and cacheable).
- **Flaky tests:** detect with re-runs, track a flake rate per test, quarantine with an owner and an SLA; never let flakiness train people to ignore red builds.
- **Test pyramid:** many unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests.

### Continuous delivery / deployment
- **Delivery** = every green build is *releasable* (deploy is one click). **Deployment** = every green build is deployed automatically.
- **Build once, promote the same artifact** through dev → staging → prod (immutable, versioned, signed). Never rebuild per environment; configuration is separate.
- **Strategies:** rolling, **blue/green** (switch traffic between two environments; instant rollback), **canary** (1% → 10% → 100% with automated analysis of error rate and latency), **feature flags** (decouple deploy from release; kill switch), shadow traffic.
- **Rollback vs roll forward;** database migrations with expand/contract (backward-compatible schema changes first).
- **GitOps:** the desired state lives in Git (e.g. Argo CD reconciles the cluster to it); every change is auditable.
- **DORA metrics:** deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore.

### Package management
- **Semantic versioning** MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; ranges (`^1.2.0`, `~1.2.0`); pre-releases.
- **Lockfiles** pin the exact resolved tree for reproducible installs (package-lock, poetry.lock, Gradle lockfiles); update them deliberately with bots (Dependabot/Renovate).
- **Dependency resolution:** the **diamond dependency** problem (A needs C 1.x, B needs C 2.x). Maven picks the "nearest wins", npm nests copies, pip/Poetry use backtracking SAT-like solvers, Go uses minimal version selection.
- **Private registries / proxies** (Artifactory, Nexus, CodeArtifact): caching, availability, internal packages, license and vulnerability scanning; protection against **dependency confusion** (pin scopes and namespaces).
- **Monorepo vs polyrepo:** atomic cross-project changes and a single version policy vs independent release cycles; monorepos need build-graph tooling (Bazel, Pants, Nx) and code ownership.

### Supply-chain security
SBOM (what's inside each artifact), artifact **signing** (Sigstore/cosign), **provenance** attestations (SLSA levels), pinned base images, secret scanning, least-privilege CI tokens (OIDC instead of long-lived keys), isolating untrusted PR builds.

### Developer experience as a platform
North-star metrics: **CI wait + run time** for the PR loop, local build time, deploy lead time, flake rate. Paved roads: golden templates, self-service pipelines, good error messages. Internal developer portals (service catalog, ownership).

### Linking to your background (useful for the leveling conversation)
You've built platforms where correctness at scale, policy enforcement and multi-team adoption mattered (compliance, access management, workflow engines). Map those to CI/CD: policy-as-code for pipelines (who can deploy what), audit trails, workflow orchestration (pipelines are DAG workflows, like the BPMN engine work), and guardrails. Then be honest about where you'd ramp up, and show how fast you learn a domain.
followups: What's the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
How would you cut median PR CI time from 40 min to 10?
Explain how a remote build cache decides a cache hit.
How do you safely roll out a breaking database schema change?

items.title: AI-assisted coding rounds: how to run them
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 2 (had to reason without AI in part 2) and Sep 7 report, Round 3 (AI is an assistant, not a replacement).
items.question: How should you use the AI assistant in LinkedIn's AI coding rounds?
items.short: You own the solution; the AI types faster. Restate the problem and design the algorithm yourself, out loud, before prompting. Use the AI for boilerplate, parsing long scenarios, test cases, and the API details you'd look up anyway. Review every line, run tests, and narrate what you're checking. Be ready at any moment to continue without it: the interviewer may switch it off to test your reasoning (it happened in the graph round).
items.answer:
### A loop that works
1. **Understand (no AI):** restate the problem, identify the core structure (graph? interval? cache?), list edge cases, agree on input/output.
2. **Design (no AI):** state the algorithm and complexity in 2–3 sentences. Get a nod from the interviewer.
3. **Generate (AI):** ask for a skeleton matching *your* design, plus tests (including edge cases you listed). Be specific: "Java, no lambdas, Dijkstra with a PriorityQueue of long[]".
4. **Verify (you):** read the code, run the tests, add a tricky case. Explain any fix you make. Never accept code you can't explain.
5. **Extend:** for each new requirement, say the design change first, then prompt.

### What interviewers score
- Problem decomposition and the algorithm choice: **yours**, not the AI's.
- Judgement: catching wrong or over-complicated AI output; knowing when to just write it yourself.
- Testing discipline and communication.

### Practice plan with this page
- Solve each focus problem once **without** AI to make sure the algorithms are yours (especially Dijkstra / state graphs and BFS).
- Then redo two of them with an AI assistant, timing yourself, practising specific prompts and reviewing the output.
- Rehearse the "explain without AI" moment: for Supply Drop II, explain the state graph on a whiteboard in under 2 minutes.
followups: What would you do if the AI's solution passes the tests but you don't understand one part? (Don't ship it: read it, simplify it, or rewrite that part.)

items.title: Staff behavioral + the leveling conversation
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 1 (manager): scope stories led to a Staff vs Senior Staff leveling discussion; Senior Staff required deeper domain expertise in the team's area. Sep 7 report also had behavioral questions.
items.question: Behavioral questions with a manager, where your examples also decide the level (Staff vs Senior Staff).
items.short: Prepare 6–8 stories with clear scope (team → org → company), your specific role, the hard decision or conflict, and measurable impact. For leveling: show scope (multi-org influence, multi-year vision) **and** depth in the team's domain. Research the team's domain beforehand (CI/CD and developer infrastructure here) and connect your experience to it explicitly. If they raise level, ask what evidence would support the higher level and offer it.
items.answer:
### Story bank (STAR, ~2 minutes each; lead with the result)
| Theme | Prompt you'll get | Story to pick |
|---|---|---|
| Scope & vision | "Tell me about the largest-scope thing you led." | A cross-org architecture you defined and drove to adoption; numbers (scale, adoption, revenue). |
| Ambiguity | "A problem with no clear owner or solution." | How you framed it, the options, the decision record. |
| Influence without authority | "You had to convince other teams." | Getting product, engineering and go-to-market aligned on one architecture. |
| Technical depth | "The hardest technical problem you solved." | A scale or correctness problem with real trade-offs (e.g. billions of items under policy). |
| Conflict / disagreement | "You disagreed with a leader or peer." | The data you brought, how you disagreed and then committed. |
| Failure | "Something that went wrong." | Own it, the fix, what you changed in the process afterwards. |
| Mentoring / multiplying | "How do you grow other engineers?" | Architecture forums, reviews, people you levelled up. |
| Delivery under pressure | "A deadline or incident." | What you cut, how you managed risk. |

Use your strongest recent material: architecture you defined and drove across orgs (access management/ABAC building blocks, archive at billion-file scale, workflow automation with embedded AI agents, AI guardrails), with concrete numbers where you have them.

### The leveling conversation
- Staff vs Senior Staff usually differ in **breadth of influence** (a group of teams vs a whole org/company) **and** in being *the* recognized expert in an area.
- The feedback in the report was: scope was there, **domain depth** in CI/CD was the gap. Prepare for both:
  1. One story clearly at Senior Staff scope (multi-org, multi-year).
  2. A crisp explanation of how your experience maps onto *their* domain (pipelines = DAG workflow orchestration; policy and compliance = deployment guardrails and audit; platform adoption = developer experience).
  3. A short, honest ramp-up plan for the domain gaps (first 90 days).
- It's fine to ask: "What would you need to see to be confident at the Senior Staff level?"

### Questions to ask them
Biggest developer-experience pain point today? How do they measure CI/CD success (queue time, flake rate, DORA)? Build vs buy (GitHub Actions, Buildkite, internal)? What would a Staff engineer own in the first 6 months?
followups: Why this team / domain? (Have a real answer that connects to platform and developer leverage.)
What would you do in your first 90 days?
